summary:
Mauritius decriminalised same-sex conduct on 4 October 2023, when the Supreme Court struck down Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 as unconstitutional and ruled that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. The provision had carried penal servitude of up to five years. Prosecutions were rare: the US State Department's 2016 country report found that sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce proceedings as an aggravating factor, although a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy. The government said in 2017 that it would not repeal the section, and a decriminalisation bill brought by former Attorney General Rama Valayden failed to pass. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, backed by Collectif Arc-en-Ciel.

No criminal provision in the sources targets gender expression. The State Department's 2016 report records harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing; no prosecution or detention of a visitor for gender-nonconforming presentation appears in the inventory.

Legal gender recognition is not available. The Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database form the framework that denies it, and a July 2021 policy brief by the Young Queer Alliance argues for recognition. The sources record no administrative route by which a trans visitor or resident can change a gender marker.

Mauritius recognises neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law cannot marry or register a partnership here. In practice, resorts are described as welcoming and non-discriminatory, and no problems have been recorded with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms.

The Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The sources do not state that gender identity falls within their scope. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Government statements say hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form. LGBTQ people may face discrimination in public hospitals in particular.

Pride has been held since 2005, organised by Collectif Arc-en-Ciel, founded the same year; the 2016 march drew more than 1,200 participants when it moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. In 2018 the march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, described as an Islamic extremist under state surveillance. Police had been deployed earlier in 2018 to protect marchers, an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support, and Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemned the anti-LGBTQ protest. The Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights.

During the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and other candidates used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech. Outright International, in an overview last updated 12 March 2026, records advances for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with progress for trans and intersex people 'less evident'. Conservative attitudes remain commonplace.

In 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan became the first transgender woman to compete in Miss Universe Mauritius. Analysis of her participation against the country's legal obstacles, published by AfricLaw in August 2024, concludes that legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate, and notes activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G.
tangentialFactors:
Intersex newborns may be registered as 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act, but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned. That regime sits alongside, and separately from, the absence of any legal gender recognition for trans people.

The Young Queer Alliance's 2021 policy brief cites the World Health Organization's ICD-11, which removed trans categories from the classification of mental disorders in 2019, in its argument that Mauritius should join the countries that recognise gender identity in law.

Polls place Mauritius among Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries, and a 2016 poll found that 49 per cent of Mauritians would like or would not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. Acceptance is described as growing particularly among the younger generation.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ people may face bullying in schools.

The Young Queer Alliance was founded on 1 September 2014 for young LGBTQ Mauritians and works on support, advocacy and anti-discrimination campaigns.

In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended its blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, although LGBTQI people have anecdotally still been prevented from donating on occasion.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains nothing on border or immigration practice: no sourced account of airport screening, pat-downs, secondary inspection or document-marker flagging affecting trans travellers entering Mauritius.

Whether the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 cover gender identity, and how they are enforced in practice, is not established by the sources.

No trans-specific violence data with a denominator appears in the inventory; the sources record no homicide or assault figures for trans people in Mauritius.

The sources do not state whether the 2021 Civil Status Act's 'undetermined' registration option is available to trans adults or only to intersex newborns.

It is not sourced whether the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling has been followed by an amendment to the Criminal Code or operates only as a reading-down of Section 250.

The anti-LGBTIQ statements made during the 2024 elections are not linked in the sources to any specific policy or enforcement outcome.
